messages.subject_clean: Analysis of Categorical Outcomes: Away from mixed-effect models and back to ANOVAs?
messages.body_plain:
Hi John, Holger, & all,

I thought I would throw in my two cents as one of the co-authors on the Barr et al. paper (which I will abbreviate as "KIM" for "Keep it Maximal"), and also from my own personal experience and perspective:

On Jul 25, 2012, at 9:52 AM CDT, John K Pate wrote:

> 
>> I guess most of the users of the list are aware of the submitted paper by Barr et al. on the use of maximal random effect structure for the evaluation of the significance of fixed effects in mixed-effect models. I personally find the paper convincing. But it leads to problems when confronted with real data and more complex designs, especially when you are dealing with categorical outcomes (lots of my work is on speech perception with a 2AFC task, so this standard for me).
>> 
>> In my experience, a model with more than 8 random slopes tends not to converge if you use the lmer function with a logistic linking function. And in speech-perception research that happens a lot, classically one presents a speech continuum in two condition, so a 2 x7 design is common (e.g., the classical Ganong-type experiments with a 7-step /s/ and /f/ continuum in  two contexts, gira.... (/f/ bias) and platypu... (/s/ bias)). A model such as the following:
>> 
>> lmer( f ~ continuum*bias + (continuum*bias|Subject), ...., family = binomial) 
>> 
>> is quite unlikely to converge.

(See a separate email for more thoughts on Holger's specific example.)

>> I asked around a bit, and I am not the only one experiencing this. If you would now even have an item effect as well, the chances of convergence are approaching zero quite quickly with models with a maximal random effect structure for subject and items.
> 
> Moreno Coco and I are currently working on evaluting a model selection
> function using Barr et al's simgen code, both on their artificial
> dataset and a more complex artificial dataset. Our more complex
> artificial dataset has one response generated by three fixed effects,
> two fixed interactions, two random slopes, and three random intercepts.
> All variables are continuous. Even when given the true generative
> structure, the maximal random effects structure did not converge once
> in 100,000 random datasets.

Yes, this is clearly a problem in practice and something that we have tried hard to acknowledge in KIM -- see in particular the "Random Effects for Control Predictors" and "Coping with Failures to Converge" sections on pp. 60-64 of the revised ms (http://idiom.ucsd.edu/~rlevy/papers/barr-levy-scheepers-tily-22-jun-2012-submitted.pdf).  Failure to converge, of course, is a property of both the objective function (the likelihood surface) and the algorithm.  There are some tweaks one can make within lme4 to do a better job of achieving convergence (up the maxIter and perhaps maxFN control parameters), but these can only take you so far in finite amounts of time.

My best impression is that many problems with convergence arise simply because the likelihood surface is very flat, perhaps often because there is not enough information in the dataset to estimate all the random effects with high confidence.  Sometimes this could be due to a problem of credit assignment between a fixed effect and its corresponding random slope.  Such situations underscore an important limitation of the popular t/z statistics widely used within lme4 for inferences about fixed effects, which is that these statistics are computed conditional on a point estimate of the random effects.  One of the beauties of traditional ANOVA is that it avoids reliance on point estimates; Baayen, Davidson, and Bates 2008 have an extremely concise and clear summary of this critical point in the
  final paragraph of page 396, which I think is often overlooked.  When the random effects cannot be estimated with high confidence, it may be dangerous to draw inferences about fixed effects based on a point estimate (even when convergence is attained).

>> In the rare case a model does converge, the fixed effects of the model lead to pretty bad predictions for the cell means. That is, usually I would like to see that the Intercept parameter of the model, if transformed back to proportions, matches the observed proportion in the cell of the design that is mapped on the Intercept. Similarly, I would like a good match between the observed proportions in the different cells of the design and the predicted proportions from the fixed effects. How does one interpret a model, that predicts quite different proportions for the different cells than the ones that are observed? 

There is a subtlety here that you should keep in mind: because the linking function is nonlinear, there is no guarantee that predictions using only the fixed effects estimates will match the marginal condition means in the data, especially when there are large random effects and/or the underlying cluster-specific means get toward the curvy part of the logistic function.  Here is a very simple example illustrating this, a case with 12 "subjects" with 3 observations each in each of two conditions, "A" and "B":

> set.seed(1)
> library(lme4)
Loading required package: Matrix
Loading required package: lattice

Attaching package: ‘lme4’

The following object(s) are masked from ‘package:stats’:

    AIC, BIC

> library(mvtnorm)
> invlogit <- 
+ function (x) 
+ {
+     ex <- exp(x)
+     ex/(1 + ex)
+     }
> 
> x <- factor(c("A","B"))
> M <- 10
> observations.per.subj <- 4
> subj <- factor(paste("S",1:M))
> trialnum <- rep(1:observations.per.subj)
> dat <- expand.grid(x=x,subj=subj,trialnum=trialnum)
> b <- rmvnorm(M,sigma=2*diag(2))
> dat$response <- rbinom(nrow(dat),1,prob=invlogit(-1+2*(x=="B") + b[cbind(dat$subj,x)]))
> m <- lmer(response ~ x + (x - 1| subj),data=dat,family="binomial")
> print(cov(b))
           [,1]       [,2]
[1,]  1.2186289 -0.6289803
[2,] -0.6289803  2.2877240
> print(m)
Generalized linear mixed model fit by the Laplace approximation 
Formula: response ~ x + (x - 1 | subj) 
   Data: dat 
   AIC   BIC logLik deviance
 100.9 112.8 -45.43    90.86
Random effects:

 subj   xA   0.41632  0.64523         
        xB   5.73066  2.39388  -0.758 
Number of obs: 80, groups: subj, 10

Fixed effects:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)  
(Intercept)  -0.5517     0.3900  -1.415   0.1572  
xB            2.2991     1.1178   2.057   0.0397 *
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1 

Correlation of Fixed Effects:

xB -0.620

This is a pretty decent model fit: the size of the random effect in the "A" condition is underestimated but that in the "B" condition is pretty well estimated and the correlation is reasonably in the ballpark.  The prediction from the fixed-effects estimate alone matches the "A" condition mean well, but is pretty far off from the "B" condition mean:

> with(dat,tapply(response,x,mean))
    A     B 
0.375 0.725 
> invlogit(fixef(m)[1] + c(0,1) * fixef(m)[2])
[1] 0.3654636 0.8516162

This situation doesn't generally arise for linear MEMs because everything is linear.  But a lot of bets are off regarding the behavior of marginal means once you introduce nonlinearities.

Exercise 8.11 in my textbook draft (http://idiom.ucsd.edu/~rlevy/pmsl_textbook/text.html) is loosely related to this issue.

>> After all, we really care about differences in the descriptive data, because usually theories predict differences between observed values in different conditions. The only reason to use inference statistics is that we need a yardstick to know what kind of difference in the descriptive data we should take seriously. So I am pretty bothered by the fact that the statistical model predicts quite different means than the ones I observe.
>> So does this mean: Back to ANOVAs with logistic or inverse-normal distribution transformation of individual cell means? This has been around for a while, under the name of Signal-detection theory, so it seems quite acceptable to me.

My example above notwithstanding, I do have to say that I have personally encountered multiple examples of "converged" maximal mixed logit models in lme4 -- sometimes with extremely simple fixed and random effects structure! -- which I simply do not trust.  My impression is that these situations arise most typically when one or more condition means is close to 0 or 1, and my guess is that in these situations the estimation problem is just inherently hard because there is simply very little information in the dataset that allows one to appropriately allocate credit between the fixed and corresponding random effects, so depending on what random-effects estimate the model happens to converge to the fixed-effect inferences can vary dramatically.  (It's possible that the approximation to the li
 kelihood used by lme4 contributes to this issue, though I don't have clear evidence on this point.)  For this reason I almost always check the results of traditional ANOVAs in these situations as well as sanity checks, since one of ANOVA's strengths is precisely that it avoids point estimates of random effects.

Alternatively one could implement MCMC sampling in BUGS or similar software, but I've found that often mixed logit models can be very slow to converge (probably due to the same credit-assignment problem).

My general take is that MEMs' greatest advantages over AN(C)OVA for many kinds of hypothesis testing are (1) the ability to handle crossed random effects, and (2) graceful treatment of imbalanced data.  In some kinds of traditional signal-detection paradigms, such as those Holger mentions, neither of these apply, so ANOVA remains a valuable workhorse.

>> Or how can we deal with failures to converge, which are quite common with categorical outcomes?
> 
> Perhaps it depends on your application. I like to look at corpus data,
> and so it is important to control for correlations due to common talker
> or common sentence. The model selection function we're evaluating is
> located at http://jkpate.net/cocoSelect.R, and perhaps it would be
> appropriate for your scenario. It does exhibit a few points of
> anticonservativity relative to the maximal random effects structure on
> the Barr et al datasets (obtaining a type I error rate of about 0.086
> with a critical value of 0.05), but manages to converge on the more
> complicated datasets.
> 
> It is, unfortunately, uncomfortably anti-conservative on the complicated
> datasets, although the anticonservativity decreases as the number of
> observations per level of each grouping factor increases. Specifically,
> type I error rates at a critical value of 0.05 range from about 0.10 to
> 0.23, depending on dataset size, whether we allow correlated slopes,
> and how significance is assessed. Specifically, forcing independent
> slopes and using mcmc is most anticonservative,

Just for clarification: I'm not sure what you mean by "forcing independent slopes" -- do you mean eliminating random slopes between predictors, so that for predictors X_1 ... X_n you'd have an lme4 random-effects specification of (1 | subj) + (0 + X_1 | subj) + ... + (0 + X_n | subj)?

> using the anova
> function is least. This forward-selection method is much less
> anticonservative than standard multiple regression, which obtains a
> type I error rate of about 0.43. 
> 
> We're still examining exactly how sensitive the type I error rate is to
> this aspect of the data (the resulting datasets become fairly large,
> with several thousand observations, making monte carlo simulations
> quite slow). 

This all sounds quite interesting, and I look forward to hearing more about the results you obtain!  For these more complex simulations I'd be especially keen to see results from analyses where random slopes (for predictors varying within-unit; random intercepts for predictors varying between-unit) for only the theoretically critical predictor(s) are included, or perhaps analyses where these random effects alone constitute the starting point 
of a forward-selection analysis.

Best & I hope these thoughts may be useful.

Roger

On Jul 20, 2012, at 4:20 AM CDT, Holger Mitterer wrote:

> Dear all,
> 
> I guess most of the users of the list are aware of the submitted paper by Barr et al. on the use of maximal random effect structure for the evaluation of the significance of fixed effects in mixed-effect models. I personally find the paper convincing. But it leads to problems when confronted with real data and more complex designs, especially when you are dealing with categorical outcomes (lots of my work is on speech perception with a 2AFC task, so this standard for me).
>

And in speech-perception research that happens a lot, classically one presents a speech continuum in two condition, so a 2 x7 design is common (e.g., the classical Ganong-type experiments with a 7-step /s/ and /f/ continuum in  two contexts, gira.... (/f/ bias) and platypu... (/s/ bias)). A model such as the following:
> 
> lmer( f ~ continuum*bias + (continuum*bias|Subject), ...., family = binomial) 
> 
> is quite unlikely to converge. I asked around a bit, and I am not the only one experiencing this.

Jumping to your postscript:

>> PS: A preemptive strike: If you want to propose the solution to treat continuum as a numerical variable, so that there would only be three random slopes to fit, read the following:
>> 
>> One obvious solution would be to treat continuum as a numerical variable, as this reduced the number of random slopes to be estimated. But this is problematic as well, because it severely constraints the possible form of the interaction. The bias is either constant (no interaction), gets larger at the /f/ end of the continuum (interaction < 0) or at the /s/ end (interaction > 0). But such a model would not be able to capture the (common) pattern that the effect of bias is maximal in the middle of the continuum.

Hmm, I'm not so sure that your pre-emptive strike has dissuaded me!  As illustrated by

  > invlogit <- function(x) { ex <- exp(x); ex/(1 + ex) }
  > X <- seq(-5,5,by=0.01)
  > plot(X,invlogit(X+1)-invlogit(X-1),type="l")

, treating continuum as a continuous variable predictor and entering its effect on the linear predictor as linear (i.e. using continuum*bias or bias/continuum in your formula specification) yields an absolute probability difference that is maximal at the middle of the continuum.  So if you're quantifying "effect of bias" by absolute probability difference, then the simple continuous-linear treatment of continuum will give you that.

I do take your point that the continuous-linear treatment of continuum *is* constraining on the shape of the bias effect -- e.g., it doesn't allow a big difference between p=0.4 and p=0.6 and no difference anywhere else -- but is there clear empirical evidence that the continuous-linear treatment is badly off for some types of speech perception data?  

> If one does not want to specify beforehand what form of interaction is possible, one can either try all kinds of complicated stuff with polynomials (I'd rather not and doubt that such an option would be easily interpretable for the field) or use the continuum as a categorical predictor, so that the fitted model can accommodate how the binary variable (the lexical bias in this case) influences the perception of the sounds for each step individually.

Yes, I agree that the fully non-parametric analysis of continuum effect you're suggesting has some benefits, but on the other hand it's throwing out a lot of knowledge available to us from signal-detection theory and the history of empirical speech-perception research!

Best

Roger

Hi Karin,

What's going on is that (i) the effect of a "0 + X" specification in a formula differs depending on whether X is a numeric variable or a factor, and (ii) lme4 requires that you specify the random-effects covariance matrix in complete "blocks" within which all correlation parameters are included.  When X is a numeric variable, you get a "no-intercept" interpretation, in a (0 + X | Subj) specification you are thus only specifying a 1x1 block of the covariance matrix and hence there are no correlation parameters.  When X is a K-level factor (for K>=2), however, a 0+X specification is effectively equivalent to dummy coding of X (instead of treatment coding when treatment coding would be used by default); you are reparameterizing your model but not reducing the number of parameters.  So you are
  entering a KxK block of the covariance matrix with k*(k-1)/2 correlation parameters.

> but I need it as a prerequisite for plotting my model data (mostly the interactions) using plotLMER (unless there was some other way of running plotLMER without prior application of pvals.fnc?).
> As some of the t-values (basically for interactions _:TimeZwT) change substantially from the model comprising random intercept and slope to the model comprising the intercept only, the corresponding confidence intervals of plotLMER based on the model without random slope are way too conservative.

Sorry, I don't use plotLMER so I'm not sure I understand what you're trying to do.  I tried tweaking the example code in plotLMER so that the model had a correlation parameter and things worked just fine:

> require("lme4", quietly=TRUE, character=TRUE)

100 100 100 100 100 100 100 100 100 100 
> xylowess.fnc(Y ~ X | Subject, data = dfr)
> # the smoother doesn't recognize the cosine function implemented in makeSplineData.fnc()
> dev.off()   
null device

> 
> dfr.lmer = lmer(Y ~ rcs(X, 5) + (X|Subject), data = dfr) ## I used a different random-effects specification here than in the documentation
> plotLMER.fnc(dfr.lmer)
effect size (range) for  rcs(X, 5) is  1.953781 
effect size (range) for  X is  1.953781 


What is it that you were trying to do that didn't work?


> Thus:
> Is there a way to tell R that I do not want it to add the correlation parameter in spite of "Time" being a factor, in order to be able to run pvals.fnc on the model comprising random intercept and 0+ slope without this mysterious correlation parameter?  Is there an older/a different version of lme4 that might be able to handle the problem?

If you really want to remove the correlation parameters, you can define individual numeric variables X_1 ... X_K for each of the K levels of your factor such that when an observation takes on level i the value of X_i is 1 and the value of X_j  is 0 for j≠i.  You can then use a random-effects specification of

  (0 + X_1 | Subj) + ... + (0 + X_K | Subj)

which will give you no correlation parameters.  But if the correlation parameters help improve your model fit that much, why not keep them in?  (And they're really not that mysterious -- Baayen 2008 has a nice discussion of them in section 7.1, for example, and in Barr, Levy, Scheepers, & Tily under review, http://idiom.ucsd.edu/~rlevy/papers/barr-levy-scheepers-tily-22-jun-2012-submitted.pdf, we discuss them on page 15.)

Best & I hope this helps!

Roger

Hi guys,

I've been trying to remain silent about this thread, as I am a reviewer on
the manuscript. However, Roger (van Gompel)'s comment is exactly why I -and
others- thought the original version of the paper was so misleading (I am
not commenting on the current version). I do not agree with Roger's
conclusion. Cases where mixed logit models do not converge or where it
overfits and leads to unreliable estimates are relatively easy to identify.
and lots of zero and low count cells are a problem for the model *for a
good reason. *The fact that ANOVA will always give you a result is *hardly *an
argument for it. This is like arguing that when you having a car that will
only start when you're breaks are working is worse than one that will
always start. This is arguably only true if you weigh having a running car
(publications) over travelling safely (figure out how the world works).
Haha, shit, this metaphor makes me look anti-risk. I am just waiting for

Hi all,

Holger brought up two issues with using LMEMs on categorical data, which 
are (1) convergence and (2) matching parameter estimates in logit space 
to the observed proportions.  As for (1), I don't have much to add to 
what has already been said.  As for (2), I would just point out that if 
you want predictions from the model to map onto the mean proportions in 
your data, you need to use a modeling approach that models the 
*marginal* rather than the *conditional* probabilities.  lme4 does the 
latter: the parameter estimates are relative to a subject with an 
assumed random effect of zero.  The prediction can differ from the mean 
of the sample, because the assumed normal distribution for random 
effects in logit space becomes skewed (toward .5) when it is projected 
onto probability space.  Note that if the overall probability of the 
behavior is .5, then the prediction from a conditional logit model will 
match the sample mean; to the extent to which the mean diverges from .5, 
the predicted value is "pulled" away from the sample mean toward .5 
(with the size of the "pull" proportional to the size of the variance).  
There is some discussion of the difference between conditional and 
marginal models in Raudenbush and Bryk's HLM book (though they call them 
"subject-specific" and "population-average" models).

Perhaps one way to easily get one's head around the difference is to 
think of two different "places" one could apply the logit link function 
in calculating the sample mean:

Conditional model: sample mean = the mean of the mean logits for each 
subject

Marginal model: sample mean = mean logit for the whole sample

It sounds like modeling the marginal means is what you want, so use GEE 
(Generalized Estimating Equations), or GMPM (Generalized Multilevel 
Permutation Models) instead of lme4.  Neither option allows for crossed 
random effects, unfortunately.  GEE models are implemented in the R 
packages geepack and yags; it is also possible to fit them in SPSS.  
GMPMs are implemented by my R package gmpm (see R-forge.org) which 
unfortunately is only available in beta version, but gives results you 
can count on for2^n factorial designs (which, since it is not yet ready 
for prime time, could at least be used as a sanity check on the output 
from GEE models).

-Dale

In response to Florian, the reason why I like F1 x F2 ANOVAs for categorical data is not because they always give me a result, but because they appear to be pretty good in terms of Type I and II error. Because mixed effect modelling is still very much under development (as Roger L. says), I am concerned that mixed effects are actually the car that drives (often like a Formula 1 car), but doesn't have brakes.
            It is of course true that we have always known that ANOVAs can strictly speaking only be used for parametric data. However, it is also well-known that they are very robust against violations. Interestingly, Christoph Scheepers and Dale Barr have simulations that show that F1 x F2 ANOVAs on arcsin transformed proportions do very well in terms of Type I and II error (similar to mixed effects with random slopes), which confirms that ANOVAs are indeed pretty robust.
            I can see several advantages to logit mixed effect modelling (at least in theory, more suitable to categorical data, better at dealing with unbalanced data sets, possibility of including continuous variables), so I agree with Roger L. that this is likely to become a very useful method. However, the method is still in its infancy, so we don't always know exactly what it does, and sometimes we get nasty surprises. For example, we used to think that including random intercepts was the right thing to do, but it appears that this is worse than F1 x F2 ANOVAs. We then thought that we should include random slopes if this improved the model, but it turns out that this is still worse than F1 x F2 ANOVAs. It seems to me that the Barr et al. paper is an important step forwards in that we now have simulations (hard evidence) that show that including random slopes is best with single-variable designs. But at the moment, it is still unclear what to do when the model doesn't converge or when we have designs with multiple variables. Barr et al. give some useful advice, but until we have further simulations, I don't think we can be very confident what the best method is. It's quite possible that we adopt a method that turns out to be worse than F1 x F2 ANOVAs again.
            It is only natural that new methods aren't immediately perfect and bring up some surprises, but I'd prefer if mixed effects were explored more thoroughly before everyone has to use them in their publications. At the moment, there is real confusion in the field, because the accepted "best" method continually changes and there are various pitfalls that researchers aren't aware of. This could be avoided if we find out more about the method first. To use another metaphor: If I buy an eye tracker, I make sure that it works properly before running an experiment, rather than that I run my experiment, publish the data and then check whether it worked properly.

Roger van Gompel

it's also known to be vulnerable to certain other types of violations,
including certain types of sphericity violations.


> Interestingly, Christoph Scheepers and Dale Barr have simulations that
> show that F1 x F2 ANOVAs on arcsin transformed proportions do very well in
> terms of Type I and II error (similar to mixed effects with random slopes),
> which confirms that ANOVAs are indeed pretty robust.

simulations that would seem to argue the opposite. Of course, ANOVA can do
all kind of things right if you have a lot of data per subject and item and
if the mean probabilities of interest are sufficiently far enough away from
0 or 1.

> (at least in theory, more suitable to categorical data, better at dealing
> with unbalanced data sets, possibility of including continuous variables),
> so I agree with Roger L. that this is likely to become a very useful
> method. However, the method is still in its infancy, so we don't always
> know exactly what it does, and sometimes we get nasty surprises. For
> example, we used to think that including random intercepts was the right
> thing to do,
>

people who do not invest the time to understand them. That's what I have
been saying during tutorials since at least 2009. In Baayen et al 2008,
FWIW Jaeger 2008 and previous papers by Baayen (e.g. 2004), random slopes
were included. Yet I've heard some other people say the same thing as you
(actually, it was Ken Forster). I've been using random slope models
whenever possible since the earliest moments I used these models. I have
been teaching them like that during tutorials. I know Harald has been doing
the same. Is there a source that I just missed? Perhaps I just missed a
publication or influential presentation that contains this (wrong)
information?

It's true that Harald has argued --and I have applied the same reasoning--
that there are situations when it's acceptable to not use random slopes (a
trade-off between Type I error rates, power, and the danger of over-fitting
[a problem the avg cognitive psychologist need not worry about]). I still
stand by that statement. Barr et al do not provide evidence to the
contrary. What they show is that IFF there are random slope variances in
the 'world' (the underlying distributions that we have sampled from) then
ignoring them is anti-conservative. That's, of course, true (by which I do
not mean to belittle their point -- there are many obvious things that need
to be said; and their paper makes additional important points). They
further argue that the cost of preparing for this 'worse' [sic] case
scenario is not that outlandishly high (i.e., the loss in power is
acceptable under many situations). In my view, that's their most important
contribution. So, their conclusion, let's prepare for this 'worse' case
since there aren't many reasons not to (at least when you stick to studying
your undergraduates and hence take your daily bath in abundant data).

To be clear, there are two issues here. One is whether it's ok to use model
comparison to determine the maximal random effect structure (Baayen) or
whether one should always keep it as maximal as possible (Barr et al).
That's a valid issue and I am glad that there is a paper that takes on this
issue. The other one is the one you raised "we used to think that including
random intercepts was the right thing to do". As far as I know, nobody ever
claimed that or taught it. One doesn't have to think for long to see why
this is wrong (and that's actually how I taught and teach it -- the
parallel between maximal random effect structures in mixed models and what
F1 and F2 are approximating is something I typically point out in the first
lecture on mixed models).

but it appears that this is worse than F1 x F2 ANOVAs. We then thought that
> we should include random slopes if this improved the model, but it turns
> out that this is still worse than F1 x F2 ANOVAs.

under certain assumptions about the world and for mixed linear models, yes.

that for mixed models, half of this discussion wouldn't happen. Many, if
not all, of the 'problems' you list above for mixed models are not a
surprise for people who've gone through the motions of learning about this
approach (admittedly an ongoing process -- as it is to a lesser extent with
ANOVA). This brings me to a point where I agree with you and where, I
guess, I have a different goal than others who have been vocal about using
mixed models: I don't think that mixed models have to become the standard
of the field. For one thing, ANOVA are easy to use and so what if they have
slightly increased error rates on certain types of data -- the real Type I
error issues are related to lax ethical standards in how report the data
(Simmons et al). Mixed models are a powerful tool that offer many
advantages that are simply not available (or only via hacks) in ANOVA --if
used carefully and by someone who knows how to use them. I personally don't
think that one should expect that more powerful will also be easier to use
(I mean a Ferrari only drives faster if you know how to switch gears ... --
argh, I hate car metaphors). This is something that changed in my thinking
(and teaching) after I started reviewing more and more papers on mixed
models.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

thanks for all the responses. The discussion somewhat strayed away,
which may be partly my fault. I was mainly interested in the analysis
of "boring" experiments with hords of undergraduates. Corpus Data are
a completely different animal. I also did not want this to become
a discussion of the merits of the "Keep it maximal" paper. The only
reason for me to write the initial question was that I was actually 
convinced by this paper, but realized that this may give rise to 
other problems (non-convergence for categorical data, no problems
with numerical data).

Concerning the dicsussion between Roger van Gompel and Florian Jaeger,
I wanted to add a couple of thoughts. First of all, I agree with Florian Jaeger
that the ANOVA with untransformed proportions or arcsine-transform is problematic.
In fact, I have cited Jaeger (2008) quite a bit and recently co-authored
a paper, where we show that an interaction actually changes direction (!) 
when the logistic tranform is applied (doi:10.1016/j.lindif.2012.05.005, see footnote 2).

But what about ANOVAs on logit or probit transformed proportions?
(0 and 1's replaced as recommended by Macmillan and Creelman in their SDT book)
Is this really so problematic?
d's are probit transformed proportions and have been analyzed with ANOVAs for ages.

If I understood Florian Jaeger correctly, he argued that the ANOVAs with ANY transformation
are problematic in any case when the proportions approach 0 and 1.
To add a thought here from SDT actually: When you are approaching proportions of zero and one,
you need to have lots of data anyway to make any reasonable estimate of the population mean.
That is, unless you have hords of undergraduate spending hours in your lab, and giving you
well above 40 datapoints per cell, you should not even try to find differences
between proportions near the margins.

Finally a historical note: I think I agree with Roger van Gompel that Mixed-Effect Models
may have been hyped quite a bit and that the manuals are less clear than those of 
SR-Research Eyetrackers (to stick with Florian Jaeger's metaphor).

Personally, I started using MEMs after looking at tables 4 and 5 in Baayen, Davidson, & Bates (JML2008),
which showed that the MCMC based p-values are better from a signal-detection point of view: 
Less False Alarms and a better Hit Rate.

However, even though this paper also advocated the use of random slopes, the paper implicitely
made them optional by suggesting the pvals.fnc() method. After all, this method requires the intercept-only model.
Moreover, the "keep it maximal" paper also cites "MEM manuals" that suggest intercept-only models.
Finally, I have heard the advice to first evaluate the fixed effects using the pvals.fnc() with a intercept-only model,
and then use model comparison to see which additional random slopes are significant.
(Again meaning that fixed effects are evaluated on the basis of the intercept-only model.)

It hence seems that the dust has not yet really settled, and reading "The manual"
on Mixed-Effect Models is less straightforward than picking up Hayes' Statistics book
or Keppel's Design and Analysis for doing ANOVAs. That is, reading "The manual" is really
not that straightforward here, given that it seems to depend on the manual one happens to come across.

This is not to say that MEM should not be used anymore.
If the maximal MEM converges and gives estimates that reasonably approximate the descriptive data, 
it is an extremely valuable tool, e.g., it allows trial-specific predictors, which are unthinkable in the ANOVA approach.

I was happy to see that Florian Jaeger said that the field should be pragmatic rather than prescriptive.
These days, there seems to be a 0.5 probability that at least one reviewer will ask for a different analysis method
(whichever one was used in the paper). In fact, a colleage of mine managed to get two decision letters
on the same day; one saying the ANOVAs are really outdated and should be replaced by MEMs; and the other
one saying that the MEMs used in the paper are really difficult to evaluate and should be replaced by ANOVAs.

Kind regards,
Holger

Hi Holger,

well put. I find myself agreeing with everything you said (incl. the fact
that MEMs are less straightforward and require more in-depth training than
ANOVA and than their manual leaves things to be desired even more so than
that of an eye-tracker). I think ANOVA over empirical logit transformed
proportions (when cases are weighted inversely to the variance of the cell
mean) are an acceptable solution. In Jaeger 2008 I focused on the fact that
even that transformation under-estimates effects close to 0 and 1, but in
practice data sets are finite and there's only so much 'resolution' in the
sample's mean proportion's anyway. That is something that I wish I had seen
more clearly back then. The reason why I prefer mixed logit models for my
own research (in most cases) is that I find it easier to get more
information out of them. I often work with continuous variables and am
interested in their shape and the shape of the interactions. That can, of
course, also be investigates in ANCOVA, but I find it more straightforward
in MEMs. I also really like the fact that we can *learn* about the random
effect structure and to what extent what random effect structures are
warranted by the data. A point that early on drew me to these models when I
read Baayen's early (2004) descriptions of them.

Florian

PS: when I wrote "boring" in that email, I immediately afterwards thought
that I should have been clearer that I meant "statistically less
challenging" ;). I run those types of experiments, too. As a matter of fact
some of my best friends are "boring" experiments.
